comment_content:
This course covers basic single-variable calculus: limits and continuity, derivatives and differentiation rules, applications of derivatives (like max/min problems, related rates, optimization, Newton's method), and a basic intro to integration, like substitution rule and integration by parts. Around 60-70% of the material overlaps with DSE M2, but the exam questions go deeper than hw rather than just calculations. Some new topics include the Squeeze Theorem, L'Hôpital's Rule, Mean Value Theorem, Linear Approximation, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
You really need to understand the concepts clearly, not just memorize steps. If your understanding is only surface-level, the exam can easily screw you up because they change the question style and test whether you actually get the theory. Don't just rely on homework. The exam is way harder.
comment_teaching:
The overall teaching quality varies a lot depending on which professor you get. For the non-L1 sections, many students report heavy mainland accents that make lectures hard to follow. Some professors I heard just read slides without much explanation, which isn't super helpful. Tutorial sessions can be more useful than lectures, especially if you get a good TA.
​
Don't rely too much on going to lectures, especially if your professor has a strong Chinglish accent that's hard to understand. It's better to self-study following the course schedule or watch Henry Cheng's lecture videos. Many students from other sections sit in on his classes or watch his recordings because he explains things way more clearly. His notes and problem sets really help your exam.
comment_grading:
This course uses absolute grading, which means your grade depends on your own score, not on how others perform. The usual breakdown is roughly: 10% homework (WeBWorK), 35% midterm, and 55% final. The typical cutoffs are around 85%+ for A range, 70-85% for B range. How much effort you put in is how much grade you get, pretty straightforward.

comment_workload:
The workload is not too heavy compared to other year-1 courses. You mainly just have weekly WeBWorK homework, which is pretty manageable. Most questions are standard, and there are unlimited attempts for each question except MCQs, so you can keep trying until you get full marks. There are also optional extra problem sets like the ones from Henry, that are more exam-level. If you want a good grade, you should do them, but overall this is not a high workload course as long as you keep up week by week.
​
Homework is easy and doesn't take much time. Just don't forget the deadlines since they're not always on Canvas. The real time investment is if you want to do well on exams, then you need to practice past papers and problem sets.

comment_content: If you studied M2 in secondary school, this course might feel more manageable right from the start, since the first few chapters mainly revisit differentiation, curve sketching, and related fundamentals—stuff you’ve already tackled. Things stay familiar until you hit linear approximation; that’s where the real challenges kick in and the pace picks up. But if you never took M2 before, expect a steeper learning curve and a tougher time keeping up with the early material. Either way, make it a priority to connect with classmates at UST who have that M2 background—they’ll be gold for study groups, quick clarifications, and surviving the jump to the harder topics!
comment_teaching: Most of the professors teaching this course are from mainland China, so you might encounter some with fairly heavy accents, especially if English isn’t their primary teaching language. It can take a week or two to get used to the pronunciation and pacing, but once you do, the content usually comes through clearly.
comment_grading: Since this is a common core course for both Engineering and Science students, the grading is notoriously competitive—everyone’s gunning for those top spots, and the curve is brutal. I managed 80% on the midterm and a solid 90% on the final exam, but even that only landed me a B+ in the end. It just goes to show how high the bar is set; you really need to be near-perfect across the board to pull an A.
comment_workload: This course only allocates 10% of the final grade to homework, even though you have to slog through around 10 challenging exercises just to secure that small portion—making it feel like a ton of effort for minimal reward. That said, I think it's still relatively better than those other nightmare courses where the workload is insane and the teaching is a complete disaster.

comment_content: The course content delivered by the professor is profoundly rigorous and intellectually stimulating, rooted in the fundamental logic of mathematics. He starts from the perspective of real number completeness, systematically deriving the entire framework of mathematical reasoning from its most basic principles. For students genuinely passionate about mathematics and pursuing in-depth academic exploration, this content is exceptionally high-quality—it builds a solid theoretical foundation that is invaluable for advanced studies or theoretical research. However, it is utterly unsuitable for students outside pure mathematics, such as those in physics, engineering, or business. The material is overly theoretical, offering little practical utility for applied fields; its value lies solely in deepening one’s understanding of mathematical fundamentals, making it irrelevant for anyone not aiming for a career in theoretical math.
comment_teaching: The professor’s teaching style is incredibly engaging and humorous, enhanced by his identity as an avid anime and manga enthusiast. His instructional methods are creative and memorable: for instance, one exam question playfully asked students to write the full names of Cauchy and Weierstrass, adding a lighthearted twist to rigorous mathematical learning. Additionally, his PPTs are designed with charming anime-style visuals, which make even abstract mathematical concepts more approachable and enjoyable. His lectures never feel tedious—he skillfully weaves humor and pop culture references into complex theories, keeping the class dynamic and maintaining students’ interest throughout. This unique blend of academic rigor and playful presentation makes his classes stand out as both informative and entertaining.
comment_grading: My experience with the course’s grading policy was extremely disappointing and unreasonable. Prior to enrolling, I heard rumors that the honors course had a generous A-range, supposedly up to 50%, which motivated me to sign up eagerly. However, after the midterm exam, the reality proved drastically different: out of 200 students, only 23 received an A+. For everyone else, grades started directly from B and declined downward, with no A- or A grades awarded between B and A+. This policy is absurdly rigid and unfair. I ranked 29th in the class, just a few points shy of the 23rd place cutoff, yet I was only given a B. Such a harsh and inflexible grading scale fails to recognize the nuanced differences in performance among students, making the initial claim of a "large A-range" misleading and frustrating.
comment_workload: The workload for this course is overwhelmingly heavy—far exceeding the combined workload of my other four courses, even by several times. The problem sets are extremely intellectually demanding, requiring hours of intense critical thinking and problem-solving that often feel mentally exhausting. Exams are equally challenging, designed to test not just basic understanding but also the ability to apply deep theoretical knowledge to highly complex scenarios. I frequently found myself spending entire weekends and late nights working on assignments and preparing for exams, sacrificing time that could have been allocated to other courses or personal pursuits. The course starts off with a rigorous introduction to limits(Chapter 1 and 2)
In chapter 1 it is the limit of sequences.
In chapter 2 it is the limit and continuity of functions, taught together in close conjunction with the idea of constant approximations.

Please do note that this is taught by Yan Min and the content and grading is only relevant to courses also taught by him
Basically math1013 with more focus on rigorous reasoning. The core principle is that for some fixed a and for any close numbers x, if f(x) and f(a) is also close, then lim x->a f(x) = f(a) is true. You will spend three months on the fancier derivations and superfluous discussions on this principle which the derivations are mainly about doing some high school algebra (like HKDSE core math), accompanied with this principle.
Don't worry, this is something that even me who only get level 4 in HKDSE M1 can understand and do well.
comment_teaching: If you want to enroll in this course but you don't have level 5 in HKDSE M2, just ask Yan Min and he will let you in. He will 100% allow you to take this course
comment_grading:
Lenient grading.
As this is an honor course if you complete all the work and have a basic understanding, you are mostly guaranteed with a-range. The exam won't be difficult, there will be questions of the past papers with only slight changes, and be sure that there will be no time pressure. The grading so lenient that it attracts those who aren't that good at mathematics like me and those can still get a-range. However, if they do 1013 they will face intense competitions and will likely only get b-range or lower due to curve grading. So I highly recommend this course to even those who are not that good at math.

Little.
One mid term exam and one final exam, and some homework per week
